_meta.purpose: The 'Other systems I built or own' section of /work/. These are real systems that do not warrant a full case study — they carry breadth, not depth. Deep work goes in src/work/ as a case study.
_meta.replaces: The legacy qa-portfolio.html and automation-projects.html pages, which duplicated each other and the case-study index.

other.title: Service virtualization for third-party dependencies
other.body: Several journeys depend on third-party services that cannot be called from a test environment: messaging providers, partner webhooks, scheduled callbacks. I built mock services that reproduce their contracts rather than their responses: signed webhook payloads verified with the same HMAC the production consumer uses, and a controllable clock so a re-engagement nudge scheduled fourteen days out can be tested in a second. The rule I settled on is that a mock which cannot fail the way the real service fails is a liability, because it teaches the suite that a whole class of error does not exist. Test-data isolation came out of the same work: timestamp-scoped assertions and a proxy that blocks writes to shared state, so a parallel run cannot poison another worker's fixtures.

other.title: Structural snapshot validation for journey configs
other.body: Chatbot journeys are JSON configuration graphs: the largest is 32 nodes across nine phases with two entry paths. They are edited by designers and engineers at the same time, across programs, and reviewing one by hand took the better part of an hour. Two mis-wiring bugs had already reached user-acceptance testing rather than review: a phase-skip edge, and a missing re-entry after a coaching branch. I extended the snapshot framework built for prompt regression to diff journey structure instead of model output: node counts per phase, edge adjacency, entry paths, button payload mappings, and re-engagement hook points. Each diff is categorised as a structural break, an edge change, a rename, or an additive change, so a reviewer now reads a change report instead of a graph.

other.title: Data platform ownership and automated validation
other.body: The analytics function came with the sole-QA role, and it turned out to be where a large share of real defects live. Dashboards are believed. A dashboard that quietly drops a segment of users is worse than one that is obviously broken, because nobody investigates it. The work here is validating the pipeline that feeds the dashboards rather than the charts themselves: reconciling event-level pulls against reported figures, and gating the reconciliation. One attribution gap I found this way was undercounting a meaningful share of users across three markets. The events existed; they just were not being attributed to a journey, so they were absent from every rollup.

other.title: First structured security testing pass
other.body: The platform handles protected health information and had never had a structured security scan. I tried to make it CI-native first: zaproxy/action-full-scan in GitHub Actions, since Playwright already ran there, then a headless Docker container for repeatability. Neither fit. Actions added credential and workflow overhead for a scan nobody wanted gating a pipeline; Docker couldn't load the JWT authentication context I'd built in ZAP's Desktop UI, a script-path resolution failure between the two environments with no clean fix. I ran the scan from ZAP Desktop instead, authenticated against the internal dashboard and the API surface, because an unauthenticated scan of a product where everything meaningful sits behind a login mostly proves the login works. Two high-severity findings came out of the first pass, both fixed within the sprint of discovery. In hindsight, for a manually-triggered scan that was never going to gate a pipeline, starting with the simplest interactive tool would have been faster than spending two attempts ruling out CI-shaped approaches that were never going to fit.

other.title: Performance baselines and trend gating
other.body: I built the platform's first load test plans, starting with a conversation-loading endpoint whose payload grew linearly with the number of active conversations in a journey. Measuring it before and after the fix closed the engineering story with a number rather than a developer's impression from a local request. The more interesting lesson came later: a nudge-trigger endpoint's p95 crept from 450ms toward an 800ms gate across six consecutive nightly runs and never once failed, because each run was judged alone. It was only visible as a slope after trend charts existed. A threshold answers whether tonight is acceptable; only a trend answers whether you are heading somewhere unacceptable.

other.title: Semantic cache and intent-classification regression suite
other.body: The response cache matches on vector similarity, not string equality, so coverage needed three behavioural tiers: exact match, near-duplicate (must still hit), and sufficiently-different (must miss and go to the LLM). Almost every real bug in this system's history has landed at the near-duplicate/sufficiently-different boundary rather than at either extreme. One was a routing bug: a near-duplicate hit against the wrong cached entry sent users expressing direct vaccination intent to informational content instead of the action-plan flow. The other was structural: a routine fastembed version upgrade changed how the model subword-tokenizes medical abbreviations, HPV among them. That shifted a set of known-equivalent phrase pairs from just above the cosine-similarity threshold to just below, flipping them from HIT to MISS with no change anywhere in the classifier or the test suite, only a dependency bump in the Lambda container. A standing set of those phrase pairs, asserted HIT for months in the tier-two suite, is what caught the flip before the image shipped.

other.title: Pre-merge micro-benchmark suite for the NLP pipeline
other.body: Production monitoring can tell you latency regressed; it can't stop a regression from merging. I built a pytest-benchmark suite that isolates each of the four classification-pipeline stages (regex pre-filter, semantic-cache lookup, the LLM call, response parsing) against a fixed synthetic corpus, gated in CI against a committed per-stage baseline. The LLM-call stage fights back: network jitter and the occasional timeout produce outlier latencies that have nothing to do with the code under test, so a raw p95 would trip the gate on noise as often as on a real regression. I run a Grubbs test to exclude timeout-driven outliers from that distribution before computing p95, which is what keeps the gate trustworthy enough that people don't route around it. It has already caught real regressions before they reached production.

other.title: Cache endpoint configuration management
other.body: Extending config management to the semantic cache's endpoint strings turned up a validation gap that logging alone couldn't close. ElastiCache Serverless publishes a multi-AZ DNS name that resolves successfully from inside and outside the Lambda VPC whether or not it is the record for the cluster you meant, so a cold-start check that only confirms the name resolves proves nothing about which cluster answered. Two incidents made that concrete: a Lambda redeploy that pointed one country's traffic at another country's cache, serving coherent but wrong-language cache hits before anomalous intent distribution surfaced it, and a staging endpoint promoted to production that fell through to live generation at a multi-hour latency cost. The fix replaced the DNS check with an actual Valkey PING against the resolved address before the cache layer is enabled for that invocation; a failed PING falls back to direct LLM classification rather than serving from an unverified cluster. That check is what cut diagnosis time for this incident class.

other.title: api-test-data-generator
other.body: A small open-source library for schema-driven test data generation, published to PyPI in February 2026 with a second release in April. It exists because the same fixture-shaping code kept being rewritten across suites, and because publishing something forces an interface decision that an internal helper never has to make. It is deliberately narrow: generate data that conforms to a schema, with control over which fields are randomised and which are pinned.

whatIOwn.title: Evaluation systems
whatIOwn.body: Golden datasets, judge design and calibration, nightly gates. The question is always the same: on what evidence do we believe this answer is safe to send?

whatIOwn.title: Production quality signal
whatIOwn.body: Sampling live traffic, judging it, routing the disagreements to people who know medicine better than I do, and feeding what they find back into the datasets.

whatIOwn.title: The test infrastructure underneath
whatIOwn.body: Playwright, API and contract suites, the CI they run in, and the discipline to retire the ones that have stopped earning their runtime.
